entry: Language family native to the northern Indian subcontinent, most of Europe, and Greater Iran. Over 3.4 billion people (42% of the global population) speak an Indo-European language as a first language, by far the most of any language family. According to an Ethnologue estimate, about 446 Indo-European languages are living, of which 313 belong to the Indo-Iranian branch. All are descended from Proto-Indo-European, a prehistoric language reconstructed by linguists and spoken sometime during the [[Neolithic]] or early [[Bronze Age]] (c. 3300 – c. 1200 BC). The academic consensus supports the Kurgan hypothesis, which places the homeland on the Pontic–Caspian steppe, associated with the [[Yamnaya culture]]. Written evidence appeared during the Bronze Age in Mycenaean Greek and the Anatolian languages Hittite and Luwian. Eight branches are still spoken, while Anatolian and Tocharian are extinct. The family was central to the development of [[Historical linguistics|historical linguistics]] as an academic discipline in the 19th century.

Fertile plain of northern South Asia, named after the Indus and Ganges river systems. It spans 700,000 sq km (270,000 sq mi) across northern, western and eastern India, eastern Pakistan, southern Nepal, Bhutan and almost all of Bangladesh, stretching from the [[Himalayas]] to the northern edge of the [[Deccan Plateau]]. Deposits from the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra formed the world's largest expanse of uninterrupted alluvium, and its rich water resources make the plain one of the world's most densely populated and intensely farmed areas. The [[Indus Valley Civilisation]] arose here, and the Mauryas and [[Kushan Empire|Kushans]] had their political centers in the region. [[Babur]] established the [[Mughal Empire]] in 1526 CE, and it ruled for almost the next three centuries. After the defeat of the Marathas, the [[British Raj]] controlled the region until Indian independence in 1947.

Hellenistic-era Greek kingdoms in the northwestern Indian subcontinent, covering most of modern-day Pakistan, parts of northwestern India and some eastern parts of Afghanistan. The kingdom was founded when the Graeco-Bactrian king Demetrius I invaded India from [[Bactria]] around 200 BC. Its rulers combined Greek and Indian languages and symbols on their coins and blended Greek and Indian ideas, a hybrid culture visible in archaeological remains. [[Menander I]], the best known of the kings, had his capital at Sakala in the [[Punjab]] (present-day Sialkot). After his death most of the empire splintered. The Indo-Greeks disappeared as a political entity around 10 AD after invasions by the Indo-Scythians, though Greek populations probably remained for centuries under later rulers, and the Western Satraps lingered on, encompassing local Greeks, until 415 AD.

Nomadic Iranian peoples of Saka and Scythian origin, also known as Indo-Sakas. They migrated from [[Central Asia]] southward into present-day Afghanistan, eastern Iran and northwestern India between the middle of the 2nd century BCE and the 4th century CE. The first Saka king in the subcontinent was Maues (1st century BCE), who established Saka power in Gandhara and the Indus Valley. The Indo-Scythians extended their supremacy over the northwest, conquering the Indo-Greeks, but were apparently subjugated by the [[Kushan Empire]] under Kujula Kadphises or [[Kanishka]]. The Saka continued to govern as satraps, forming the Northern and Western Satraps. Their power declined in the 2nd century CE after defeat by the Satavahana emperor Gautamiputra Satakarni. Rule in the northwest ended when the last Western Satrap, Rudrasimha III, was defeated by the Gupta emperor [[Chandragupta II]] in 395 CE. Ancient historians including Arrian and [[Ptolemy|Claudius Ptolemy]] described the Sakas as nomadic.

Armed conflict and diplomatic struggle between the [[Indonesia|Republic of Indonesia]] and the Dutch Empire, also known as the Indonesian War of Independence. Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaimed independence on August 17, 1945, and the struggle ended when the [[Netherlands]] transferred sovereignty over the [[Dutch East Indies]] to the Republic of the United States of Indonesia at the end of 1949. The four-year struggle combined sporadic but bloody armed conflict, internal political and communal upheavals, and two major international diplomatic interventions. Dutch forces controlled the major towns and industrial assets of [[Java]] and [[Sumatra]] but not the countryside. By 1949, international pressure, including threats by the [[United States]] to cut off economic aid for postwar reconstruction in the Netherlands, and a partial military stalemate forced the transfer. The revolution ended colonial administration except in Dutch New Guinea and reduced the power of many local rulers, but did not significantly improve the economic or political fortunes of most Indonesians.

Official and national language of Indonesia, a standardized variety of [[Malay language|Malay]]. It has been used as a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] across the Indonesian [[Archipelago|archipelago]] for centuries. According to Indonesia's 2025 Intercensal Population Survey (SUPAS 2025), 98.12% of Indonesians are fluent in it, making it the largest language by number of speakers in [[Southeast Asia]]. Its vocabulary draws on regional languages such as Javanese, Sundanese, Minangkabau and Balinese, and on foreign languages including Arabic, Dutch, Portuguese, [[Sanskrit]] and English. Most Indonesians also speak one of more than 700 indigenous languages at home, but formal education, nearly all national [[Mass media|mass media]], governance and the judiciary use Indonesian. It was the official language of East Timor under Indonesian rule from 1976 to 1999, and in November 2023 it was recognized as one of the official languages of the [[UNESCO]] General Conference.

Largest city of the Indian state of [[Madhya Pradesh]] and administrative headquarters of its district and division. Established on the banks of the Kanh and Saraswati rivers, Indore traces its roots to a 16th-century founding as a trading hub between the [[Deccan Plateau]] and [[Delhi]]. It came under the [[Maratha Empire]] after the conquest of Malwa by Peshwa Baji Rao I, and was later annexed by the [[East India Company|British East India Company]]. Before Indian independence it was the Kingdom of Indore, a nineteen-gun salute princely state of the [[British Raj]] ruled by the Holkars. The metropolitan region, which includes Ujjain and Pithampur, had an estimated population of 5.6 million in 2025 and is a major center for pharmaceutical and automotive manufacturing. The city is home to an Indian Institute of Technology and an Indian Institute of Management, and it is consistently ranked India's cleanest city.

Vedic god of weather, considered the king of the devas in Hinduism. He is associated with the sky, [[Lightning|lightning]], [[Thunder|thunder]], storms, rains and war. Indra is the most frequently mentioned deity in the *Rigveda*. He killed the asura Vritra, who obstructed human prosperity, and thereby brought rain and sunshine as the savior of mankind. His significance diminishes in post-Vedic literature, and in [[Buddhism]] he is reduced to a figurehead who suffers rebirth. He wields the vajra and rides the elephant Airavata. He resembles [[Zeus]], [[Jupiter (god)|Jupiter]] and [[Thor]] as a thunder god of Proto-Indo-European mythology.

Property of an electrical conductor that opposes changes in the electric current flowing through it. The current generates a magnetic field, and any change in that field through a circuit induces a voltage, a process known as [[Electromagnetic induction]]. This induced voltage opposes the change, as stated by Lenz's law, and is called back EMF. Inductance is defined as the ratio of induced voltage to the rate of change of current, and depends on the geometry of the conductor and the magnetic permeability of nearby materials. A component designed to add inductance to a circuit is an [[Inductor]]. The term was coined by Oliver Heaviside in May 1884. The SI unit is the henry (H), which produces one [[Volt|volt]] of induced voltage when the current changes at one [[Ampere|ampere]] per second. It is named after Joseph Henry, who discovered inductance independently of [[Michael Faraday|Faraday]].

Method of logical reasoning in which the conclusion of an argument is supported with some degree of probability but not deductive certainty. Unlike [[Deductive reasoning|deductive reasoning]], where the conclusion is certain if the premises are correct, inductive conclusions are at best probable. Types include generalization, prediction, statistical syllogism, argument from analogy and causal inference. A statistical generalization infers a conclusion about a population from a random sample, and is reliable within a margin of error when the sample is genuinely random and large. Hasty generalization and the biased sample are fallacies of generalization. Probabilities can be estimated with techniques such as [[Bayesian inference]]. [[Aristotle]] distinguished induction as a move from particulars to universals, [[Francis Bacon]] advocated empirical induction for science, and [[David Hume]] questioned why past patterns justify future expectations. [[John Stuart Mill]] later refined inductive methods such as agreement and difference.

Passive two-terminal electrical component that stores energy in a magnetic field, also called a coil, choke or reactor. It typically consists of an insulated [[Wire|wire]] wound into a coil. When the current through it changes, the changing magnetic field induces a voltage that opposes the change, so inductors resist changes in current. Its [[Inductance|inductance]] is measured in henries (H), named after American scientist Joseph Henry. Many inductors have a core of iron or ferrite, which increases the magnetic field and inductance. Along with [[Capacitor|capacitors]] and [[Resistor|resistors]], inductors are one of the three passive linear circuit elements. They are widely used in [[Alternating current|alternating-current]] equipment, particularly [[Radio|radio]] equipment, where chokes block alternating current while allowing direct current to pass. Values typically range from 1 μH (10⁻⁶ H) to 20 H.

Transboundary river of South and Central Asia, 3,180 km (1,980 mi) long. It rises in the [[Tibet Autonomous Region]] of China, flows northwest through the disputed [[Kashmir]] region, then turns south through [[Pakistan]] and empties into the [[Arabian Sea]] near [[Karachi]]. The river drains about 1,120,000 sq km (430,000 sq mi) and carries an estimated 175 km³ a year (5,500 m³/s), making it one of the 50 largest rivers in the world by average annual flow. The [[Indus Valley Civilisation]] rose along its banks in the 3rd millennium BC, and the *Rigveda* and the *Avesta* both name the Punjab region with terms meaning "seven rivers." The river entered Western knowledge when King Darius of Persia sent his Greek subject Scylax of Caryanda to explore it, c. 515 BC.

Process of identifying problems and creating products, systems and experiences that make everyday activities more efficient or meaningful. As an applied art, industrial design combines aesthetics and user-focused considerations with form, function, ergonomics, marketing, brand development, sustainability and sales. The designer determines a product's form and features before manufacture, whereas in craft-based design the maker determines form largely during production. The discipline is linked to the [[Industrial Revolution]] in Great Britain in the mid-18th century, which changed how objects were made, while [[Urbanization|urbanization]] and a wider [[Middle class|middle class]] created demand for fashionable styles. Earlier, the Gobelins Manufactory, opened in [[Paris]] in 1667 by [[Louis XIV]], produced sumptuously decorated products under royal patronage. In the 20th century Walter Dorwin Teague founded the firm TEAGUE in 1926, and Henry Dreyfuss became the first president of the Industrial Designers Society of America when it was established in 1965.

Branch of engineering concerned with the optimization of complex processes, systems and organizations. It designs, improves and installs integrated [[System|systems]] of people, materials, information, equipment and energy, drawing on the [[Mathematics|mathematical]], physical and social sciences. Industrial engineers work to reduce waste and raise [[Productivity|productivity]] and quality, using principles such as lean manufacturing and Six Sigma. They are employed in [[Manufacturing|manufacturing]], healthcare, [[Logistics|logistics]], [[Finance|finance]] and education. The field grew out of factory systems and mass production. Frederick Taylor, often called the "father of industrial engineering", emphasized time studies and standardized work methods in principles published in 1911. Frank and Lillian Gilbreth developed motion studies, and the American Institute of Industrial Engineering was founded in 1948. The discipline overlaps with [[Operations research]], systems engineering and ergonomics.

Robot used for [[Manufacturing|manufacturing]], automated, programmable and capable of movement on three or more axes. Typical applications include [[Welding|welding]], painting, assembly, pick and place for [[Printed circuit board|printed circuit boards]], packaging, palletizing and inspection, all with high endurance, speed and precision. The most common type is the articulated robot, which resembles a human [[Arm|arm]] and has several degrees of freedom. Other types include Cartesian, cylindrical, spherical, SCARA and delta robots. The foundational [[Patent|patent]] was filed by George Devol in 1954, and the first Unimate was installed in 1961 at a [[General Motors]] die-casting plant in New Jersey. In 2024, an estimated 4,663,698 industrial robots were in operation worldwide, according to the International Federation of Robotics.

Period of social and economic change that transforms an agrarian and feudal society into an industrial one. It involves an extensive reorganization of an economy for manufacturing, and is associated with polluting industries dependent on [[Fossil fuel|fossil fuels]]. With the focus on sustainable development, it increasingly includes technological leapfrogging. The first phase, the [[Industrial Revolution]], began in Great Britain in the mid-18th century and spread to Belgium, Switzerland, Germany and France. The [[Second Industrial Revolution]] followed the refinement of the [[Steam engine|steam engine]], the internal combustion engine and electricity, and the assembly line gave it a boost. Industrialization changed family structures as extended families stopped living together, though historians widely contest the theory of [[Talcott Parsons]] that it created the nuclear family. Workers moved to cities, increasing urbanization and the spread of disease, and industrialization contributed to [[Child labour|child labor]]. By the end of the 20th century, [[East Asia]] had become one of the most recently industrialized regions.

Mathematical relation making a non-equal comparison between two numbers or other expressions. Inequalities most often compare two numbers by their size on the number line. The main types are less than (<) and greater than (>), which exclude equality, and the non-strict less than or equal to (≤) and greater than or equal to (≥). The notation a ≠ b means that a is not equal to b. In engineering, a ≪ b means that a is much less than b, normally by several orders of magnitude. An inequality is preserved under [[Addition|addition]] and [[Subtraction|subtraction]] of a common constant, and under multiplication or [[Division (mathematics)|division]] by a positive number, but multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses it. Reversing the two quantities while flipping the symbol gives an equivalent statement.

Fundamental principle of classical physics, the tendency of an object to stay at rest or in uniform motion unless a force changes its velocity. Inertia is one of the primary manifestations of [[Mass|mass]], and [[Isaac Newton]] described it as his first law of motion. In his 1687 work *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, Newton defined inertia as the innate power of matter to resist changes in its state. On Earth, [[Friction|friction]] and [[Gravity|gravity]] often mask inertia, which led [[Aristotle]] to conclude that moving objects come to rest unless a force keeps them moving. [[Lucretius]] argued that motion, not stasis, was the default state of matter. The principle was first articulated by [[Galileo Galilei]] in the early 17th century through thought experiments on objects that continue indefinitely without friction.

Type of soldier who specializes in ground combat, typically fighting dismounted. Historically the term described foot soldiers who marched and fought on foot. Modern usage covers light, heavy, mountain, motorized, mechanized and airborne infantry, among other subtypes. Infantry were the first military forces in history, armed with a [[Spear|spear]], [[Axe|axe]], [[Sword|sword]], javelin, [[Sling (weapon)|sling]] or bow. Dragoons were created as mounted infantry, and from about the mid-19th century, as [[Firearm|firearms]] grew more effective, [[Cavalry|cavalry]] increasingly fought dismounted and most transitioned to mounted infantry. Mechanized infantry ride in armored personnel carriers and, in some forces, infantry fighting vehicles approaching light tanks. The term infantryman was not coined until 1837. Infantry remain indispensable for tasks such as urban clearance and holding key objectives.

Common viral infection, also called glandular fever, usually caused by the [[Epstein–Barr virus]]. Most people are infected as children, when it causes few or no symptoms. In young adults it often causes fever, sore throat, swollen neck lymph nodes and fatigue, and most people recover within two to four weeks, although fatigue may last months. The [[Spleen|spleen]] may swell, and splenic rupture occurs in less than one percent of cases. It spreads mainly through saliva. There is no [[Vaccine|vaccine]], and treatment is supportive, with fluids, rest and pain relievers such as [[Paracetamol|paracetamol]] and [[Ibuprofen]].

Step in logical reasoning, moving from premises to logical consequences. Inference is traditionally divided into deduction and induction, a distinction that dates at least to [[Aristotle]] (300s BC). Deduction draws conclusions that follow from premises assumed to be true, and the laws of valid inference are studied in [[Logic|logic]]. [[Inductive reasoning|Induction]] moves from particular evidence to a universal conclusion, which is probable but not certain. A third type, abduction, proposed notably by [[Charles Sanders Peirce]], seeks a best explanation based on likelihood. Statistical inference draws conclusions under uncertainty from quantitative or categorical data subject to random variation. In [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]], inference means applying a trained model to new data to generate outputs. An argument can be valid even if its parts are false, and invalid even if some parts are true.

First part of the 14th-century *Divine Comedy* by [[Dante Alighieri]]. It describes a fictionalized Dante's journey through [[Hell]], guided by the Roman poet [[Virgil]]. Hell is depicted as nine concentric circles of torment within the Earth, reserved for those who yield to bestial appetites or violence, or who pervert their intellect to fraud or malice. As an allegory, the *Divine Comedy* represents the soul's journey toward [[God]], with the *Inferno* describing the recognition and rejection of sin. Many but not all scholars agree that it was begun in 1306–1307 and completed in 1309–1310, though revisions continued for years.

Inability of a male or female organism to reproduce. In humans, infertility is defined as the inability to become pregnant after at least one year of regular unprotected [[Sexual intercourse|sexual intercourse]]. Estimates from 1997 suggested that about five percent of heterosexual couples worldwide had an unresolved problem with infertility, and the [[World Health Organization]] reported in 2023 that about 17.5% of people experience infertility during their lifetime. Male infertility accounts for 20–30% of cases, female infertility for 20–35%, and combined problems in both partners for 25–40%; no cause is found in 10–20%. The most common causes of female infertility are hormonal, including low [[Estrogen|estrogen]]. Fertility declines with age as ovarian follicles and oocytes decline, and [[Endometriosis]] accounts for 25–40% of female infertility. Male infertility is most commonly due to deficiencies in [[Semen|semen]] quality.

Violation of a couple's emotional or sexual exclusivity, also called adultery, cheating or having an affair. What constitutes infidelity depends on the expectations within a relationship; in [[Marriage|marriage]], exclusivity is commonly assumed. It often provokes [[Anger|anger]] and sexual [[Jealousy|jealousy]], and can cause psychological harm including betrayal, depression, low confidence and even [[Post-traumatic stress disorder|post-traumatic stress disorder]]. The Kinsey Reports of the early 1950s found that around half of men and a quarter of women studied had committed adultery. Data from the [[University of Chicago]]'s General Social Survey, taken since 1972, indicate that about 12% of men and 7% of women admit to an extramarital relationship. Infidelity frequently leads to [[Divorce|divorce]], and over half of affected marriages end that way.

Novel by American writer [[David Foster Wallace]], published in 1996. Often considered Wallace's magnum opus, the book is an encyclopedic novel with an unconventional structure and hundreds of endnotes. It is set in a near-future North America, where the United States, Canada and Mexico form the Organization of North American Nations. Its plot follows students at a [[Tennis|tennis]] academy and a substance-abuse recovery facility, and centers on a lethally entertaining film cartridge. The title comes from *Hamlet*. The novel sold 44,000 hardcover copies in its first year and has since sold more than a million copies worldwide.
